a42.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a42.speech: Said governments in sub-Saharan Africa have provided school meals to roughly 20 million extra children over the past two years, showing a move away from dependence on foreign aid. "Government investments in school meals … (signal) a significant shift from reliance on foreign aid to recognising school meals as a strategic public investment in children's education (and) health," the report said.

a42.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP report)
a42.speech: Warned that millions of children, especially in some of the lowest income African countries like the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Somalia, and South Sudan, still lacked access to school meals, as donor support continued to fall.

a42.speaker: United Nations (U.N. report, late July)
a42.speech: Found that more than one in five Africans, 307 million, were chronically malnourished, meaning hunger is worse than two decades ago. Predicted the continent would have 60% of the world's hungry people by 2030.

a69.speaker: Arab leaders who met with Trump (letter)
a69.speech: Sent Trump a letter asking the president-elect "to apply [his] political influence in demanding an immediate ceasefire in Lebanon and Palestine" with a view towards negotiating "a lasting peace."

a254.speaker: Numene Bartekwa, Grand Kru County Senator
a254.speech: Moved the motion following which members of the Liberian Senate took the decision late Friday, December 20, 2024 to concur with the House Majority bloc on the passage of the Fiscal Year 2025 National Budget of US$880.07 million.

a254.speaker: J. Fonati Koffa, embattled Speaker of the House of Representatives
a254.speech: Described both the Senate and the Majority bloc action on the passage of the 2025 National Budget as ultra vires ; labeled the passage of the 2025 National Budget by the two legislative chambers as ultra vires.

a254.speaker: J. Fonati Koffa, embattled Speaker of the House of Representatives
a254.speech: Termed his removal by the majority bloc, which voted in November to remove him as Speaker, illegal.

a259.speaker: Fatime Boukar Kossei, Chadian Minister of Humanitarian Affairs
a259.speech: Emphasized the importance of this project in providing support to the most vulnerable and ensuring a better future for those affected by the conflict.

a437.speaker: OCP Africa (post on the X platform)
a437.speech: Explained that this approach aims to respond to local agricultural challenges while stimulating sustainability and economic growth.

a437.speaker: Speakers at the launch ceremony (more than 40 key stakeholders attending)
a437.speech: Highlighted the strategic role of these centres in transforming agricultural practices in Rwanda.

a474.speaker: Endeavour Mining (press release published 6 June 2024)
a474.speech: Reaffirmed its firm commitment to reducing the impact of its activities on the environment, in line with its sustainable development strategy, saying it is aware that the sustainability of its activities rests on responsible management of natural resources; the company sets itself a target of protecting and preserving 1,800 hectares and rehabilitating 300 hectares in West Africa between 2024 and 2026, and states that through its foundation the mining group “has been able to reforest more than 80 hectares since 2023 as part of a partnership with the NGO YeS Fondation”; according to the note, the partnership signed in Côte d’Ivoire with the Jean Lorougnon Guédé University of Daloa aims to build an “arboretum” dedicated to the conservation of rare botanical species and the promotion of scientific programmes for endangered species.

a474.speaker: Djaria Traoré, Executive Vice-President for Sustainable Development and Supply Chain, Endeavour Mining
a474.speech: Said she was proud to contribute, through the group’s actions, to the “restoration of land” – the theme chosen this year for the celebration of World Environment Day, which echoes the 15th United Nations Sustainable Development Goal, namely the protection of terrestrial fauna and flora.

a504.speaker: Anthony Kasunda, presidential press secretary
a504.speech: Said the two ministers briefed the President on "measures being taken" to investigate the violence, following Chakwera's earlier directive while in Nigeria.

a504.speaker: Human rights advocates and political analysts
a504.speech: Say the President's move is cosmetic and reactionary—falling far short of the decisive action Malawians expected.

a504.speaker: Wonderful Mkhutche, political analyst
a504.speech: "What is there to investigate when the attackers were caught on camera?" ; "If the government was serious, arrests would have already been made."

a504.speaker: Robert Mkwezalamba, Human Rights Consultative Committee chairperson
a504.speech: Slammed the delay as a dangerous signal of tolerance for impunity: "The President should have fired the Inspector General and army commander by now. That would show he means business."

a504.speaker: Mabvuto Bamusi of the Political Science Association
a504.speech: Called the presidency's response "a disappointing cover-up" and "a victory for the panga-wielding thugs."

a504.speaker: Local and international bodies, including the European Union
a504.speech: Condemned the violence and threatened aid cuts.

a504.speaker: Police
a504.speech: Claim investigations are still ongoing—despite clear video evidence and eyewitness accounts.

a876.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a876.speech: When he regained the American presidency a few months ago, announced some radical measures aimed at making America great again.

a876.speaker: Other donors, including the United Kingdom
a876.speech: Have also warned that aid will no longer be a priority.

a876.speaker: United States government
a876.speech: Only last week, announced a sudden termination of funding from the Millennium Challenge Corporation.

a876.speaker: Trump administration
a876.speech: Has made it clear that it views us [Malawi] as careless and irresponsible.

a876.speaker: US Embassy in Malawi
a876.speech: Listening to the statements made by the US Embassy [on the denial of American visas to so-called “Malawian diplomats”], one cannot help but feel shame upon realising that our systems are so porous that even our approach to diplomacy cannot be trusted.

a955.speaker: Hamza Adan Haadoow, Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of the Federal Government of Somalia, and Dr. Abdallah Al Dardari, UN Assistant Secretary General, UNDP Assistant Administrator and Director of the Regional Bureau for Arab States
a955.speech: Both sides underscored the importance of transitioning from humanitarian assistance to sustainable development, aiming for long-term prosperity.

a1045.speaker: Gabriel Degbegni, Coordinator of the Millennium Challenge Account Benin II (Mca-Benin II) programme
a1045.speech: Informed the opening of the 24th ordinary board session that the last three months of implementation of Mca-Benin II projects ended with a commitment rate of about "51%" and a disbursement rate of "more than 70%", figures that are "clearly improved compared with previous quarters"; since the programme began, commitment and disbursement rates of financial resources are assessed at "86% and 48%" respectively.

a1045.speaker: Gabriel Degbegni, Coordinator of the Millennium Challenge Account Benin II (Mca-Benin II) programme
a1045.speech: Speaking about the ongoing worksites, announced the completion of certain power line works by December 2021 and of several electrical substations for the first quarter of 2022, while certain worksites would be delayed because of the many difficulties encountered on the ground, namely the harmful effects of Covid-19, the poor performance of some companies, the weak responsiveness of stakeholders and the numerous changes made to the initial scope of works; the schedule slippage concerns the substations to be built at Vedoko, Maria-Gleta, Bohicon, Parakou, Djougou and Natitingou, which will be completed in the second half of 2022 according to the new projections.

a1045.speaker: Gabriel Degbegni, Coordinator of the Millennium Challenge Account Benin II (Mca-Benin II) programme
a1045.speech: Drew the board's attention to the challenges to be met regarding the continued implementation of off-grid electricity access projects, adding: "I know that the national coordination will continue to benefit from your support in meeting these challenges, and from your valuable guidance and recommendations with a view to completing all planned activities on time."

a1068.speaker: Government of South Africa
a1068.speech: Expressed concern about the safety of its nationals and of the other participants aboard the Global Sumud Flotilla, after reports of Israeli naval interceptions and drone activity near the civilian convoy currently sailing in the Mediterranean Sea; South Africa once again called for restraint, warning against any unilateral action likely to worsen tensions or endanger lives.

a1068.speaker: South African Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) (statement)
a1068.speech: In a statement released on Thursday, said it was closely following the situation, stressing that the safety and physical integrity of all the unarmed participants - including South African citizens - remained an absolute priority. "Any military intervention or forced detention of these vessels in international waters would constitute a serious violation of international legal norms and of fundamental human rights," the department warned, calling on all parties to strictly respect international law, in particular the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the relevant humanitarian principles.

a1191.speaker: Edmund Yakani, Executive Director of Community Empowerment for Progress Organization (CEPO)
a1191.speech: Said the closure of embassies and consulates by South Sudan's traditional allies reflects their disappointment with lack of commitment from the country's political leaders to deliver lasting peace; in a statement shared with Eye Radio said the trend of closure of diplomatic missions in South Sudan is an expression of great disappointment, and stated that the main concern the foreign nations may not have expressed is the sluggish efforts by South Sudanese leaders in transitioning the country from chronic violence to peace. "I take this opportunity to amplify my voice loudly to the attention of the leaders in South Sudan on a new trend that we have seen." ; "Our traditional friends from other parts of the world are now deciding to close down their embassies under the pretext that they are closing their embassies because they want to cut down their foreign spending." ; "I'm quite sure the message of where the traditional friends of South Sudan are closing their diplomatic mission in South Sudan is an expression of great disappointment. Why the great disappointment? Because as a country, we have seen dragging of feet in transitioning the country from violence to peace without any clear commitment and a will from our leaders." ; Suggested a need for South Sudan to have a change of strategy and approach with regard to the political transitional process: "Dragging feet to transition the country from violence to peace, may lead us to a situation of isolation by our traditional friends."

a1191.speaker: Edmund Yakani, Executive Director of CEPO
a1191.speech: "On a separate note, I would like to alert every South Sudanese. Whoever you are with whatever power you hold, please abstain from weaponizing information to meet your own political objective." ; "Weaponizing information with loaded hate speech, hostile propaganda, fake news, disinformation, with misinformation, is a crime. And we have seen a trend where some South Sudanese are start weaponizing information."

a1191.speaker: Cabinet of the Kingdom of the Netherlands
a1191.speech: Approved on April 17 a proposal by the country's foreign minister to close embassies in South Sudan and other parts of the world, reportedly as part of a broader budget reduction policy and to reshape its global diplomatic presence.

a1191.speaker: German Federal Foreign Office
a1191.speech: Decided to let its diplomatic mission in South Sudan temporarily operate from Berlin, although it added that the mission may resume operations in Juba as soon as conditions permit.

a1191.speaker: Michael J. Adler, United States Ambassador to South Sudan
a1191.speech: Said on April 29 that the Embassy in Juba remains operational although the staff number has been severely reduced.

a1191.speaker: Media reports (April 15)
a1191.speech: Reported that Washington was weighing closing nearly 30 overseas embassies and consulates including in South Sudan, as it eyes significant changes to its diplomatic presence abroad.

a1191.speaker: Jok Madut Jok, renowned South Sudanese academic
a1191.speech: Said should Washington proceed with the plan, it would be bad news for South Sudanese and undermine America's ability to monitor and address negative developments in the country.

a1221.speaker: The Japan Times (headline/report)
a1221.speech: A headline reported that Japanese citizens were voicing concerns about their prefectures being "assigned" African countries under the Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD) exchange framework.

a1241.speaker: Unidentified armed men (notices posted in shops at the Zimpeto Wholesale Market)
a1241.speech: In all the shops, the men posted papers with information ordering traders to close their shops on Saturdays by 13:30 and prohibiting opening on Sundays; the information varies from shop to shop, with some ordered to close their establishments early and others to immediately reduce the prices of basic necessities.

a1241.speaker: Omar, trader at the Zimpeto Wholesale Market
a1241.speech: Is already considering the possibility of closing his shop and stopping business until the situation returns to normal.

a1287.speaker: Francis Bacon
a1287.speech: There are "some books to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested".

a1287.speaker: John Perkins, author of 'Confessions of an Economic Hit Man' and former Economic Hit Man
a1287.speech: said that it was very difficult for him to publish this book. First, he could not get daring publishers. But Perkins did not accept the advice to fictionalize it.

a1287.speaker: A man at a publishing house owned by a powerful international corporation
a1287.speech: read the draft and said, "a riveting story that needs to be told". But fearing for bad reactions from his big bosses, he advised Perkins to fictionalize it.

a1287.speaker: A reader of the book
a1287.speech: "Perkins reveals shocking details of how United States Government and corporate America work hand in hand in maintaining a dominating role in international affairs by using greed and corruption to inhibit foreign governments from economic development".

a1287.speaker: John Perkins, author of 'Confessions of an Economic Hit Man'
a1287.speech: tells us that EHMs are highly paid professionals who cheat countries around the globe out of trillions of dollars. They funnel money from World Bank, the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and other foreign "aid" organizations into the coffers of huge corporations and the pockets of a few wealthy families who control the planet's natural resources.

a1287.speaker: John Perkins's immediate boss
a1287.speech: You "are paid to cheat countries around the globe out of billions of dollars. A large part of your job is to encourage world leaders to become part of a vast network that promotes U.S. commercial interests. In the end, those leaders become ensnared in a web of debt that ensures their loyalty. We can draw on them whenever we desire – to satisfy our political, economic, or military needs. In return, these leaders bolster their political positions by bringing industrial parks, power plants, and airports to their people. Meanwhile, the owners of U.S. engineering and construction companies become very wealthy".

a1287.speaker: John Perkins, author of 'Confessions of an Economic Hit Man'
a1287.speech: recounts in his book: "Like our counterparts in the Mafia, EHMs provide favors. These take the form of loans to develop infrastructure – electric generating plants, high ways, ports, air ports, or industrial parks". The loan given by WB "never leaves the United States; it is simply transferred from banking offices in Washington to engineering offices in New York, Houston, or San Francisco". ; "When this happens, then like the Mafia we demand our pound of flesh. This often includes one or more of the following: control over United Nations votes, the installations of military bases, or access to precious resources such as oil…" In this way "the global empire demands its pounds of flesh in the form of oil concessions."

a1287.speaker: Jaime Roldos, President of Ecuador
a1287.speech: warned all foreign interests, including but not limited to oil companies, that unless they implemented plans that would help Ecuador's people, they would be forced to leave his country.

a1287.speaker: Omar Torrijos, General and leader of Panama
a1287.speech: insistently demanded America relinquish the Panama Canal to its rightful owners. ; "Omar Torrijos… confessed to having nightmares about his own assassination; he saw himself dropping from the sky in a gigantic fireball."

a1287.speaker: John Perkins, author of 'Confessions of an Economic Hit Man'
a1287.speech: Expressing the atrocious acts, Perkins says, "The U.S. army had prohibited the press, the Red Cross and other outside observers from entering the heavily bombarded areas [of Panama] for three days, while soldiers incinerated and buried the causalities."

a1305.speaker: Bank of Namibia
a1305.speech: Has warned of potential economic repercussions for Namibia following the United States' decision to suspend foreign aid to numerous countries, including those in Africa.

a1305.speaker: Johannes !Gawaxab, Bank of Namibia Governor
a1305.speech: Said the move could significantly affect Namibia due to its currency's peg to the South African rand and the close trade relationship between South Africa and the US. Speaking at the monetary policy announcement: “We need to watch the trade relations and the exchange rate movements, and see what the impact thereof is on the Namibian economy, especially the relationship between South Africa and the US, which will have a profound impact on the Namibian economy.” ; Highlighted the substantial presence of US companies in South Africa: “I understand there are about 600 US companies doing business in South Africa, and those companies employ about 200 000 people in SA.” ; Pointed out that trade relations between South Africa and the US account for approximately 5% of South Africa's GDP ; While acknowledging that it is too early to determine the full extent of the impact, stressed the importance of monitoring the situation closely: “So far, there are no policies implemented; It's too early to tell, so we need monitor how that will fit into our inflation, growth and the Southern African Customs Union (Sacu) revenue in the next few years.” ; Noted the presence of “quite a lot of policy uncertainty” and the necessity for close monitoring of the situation.

a1305.speaker: Johannes !Gawaxab, Bank of Namibia Governor
a1305.speech: On the repo rate decision: “Commercial banks are accordingly expected to reduce their lending rates by 25 basis points, bringing their prime rate to 10.50%. The newly adopted policy stance will continue safeguarding the one-to-one link between the Namibia dollar and the rand while supporting domestic economic activity.”

a1305.speaker: Simonis Storm (recent report)
a1305.speech: Stated that Namibia faces a complex trade outlook in 2025, as its economy is significantly influenced by regional and global dynamics: “Given Namibia's deep integration with South Africa through, economic pressures in South Africa, exacerbated by global trade disruptions and US tariff policies, could significantly impact Namibia. As Namibia's largest trade partner, South Africa's economic health has direct implications for Namibia's trade dynamics.” ; The company said a slowdown in South Africa could weaken demand for Namibian exports, particularly in key sectors like mining, agriculture and manufacturing.

a1305.speaker: Simonis Storm (recent report)
a1305.speech: “Currency volatility also poses a risk. The Namibia dollar's peg to the rand means fluctuations in the rand directly impact Namibia's trade position. A weaker rand could increase the cost of imports, raising inflation and squeezing household purchasing power. However, it could also boost Namibia's export competitiveness, making products like diamonds, uranium and fish more attractive on global markets.”

a1305.speaker: Joseph Sheehama, independent researcher
a1305.speech: Said a rate cut was widely expected, given that inflation declined to 3.2%, and also positive international reserves ; “Now is the time to pay off your debt more quickly. If you currently have a large amount of debt to manage, now is a good time to think about obtaining what are known as consolidation or restructuring loans. When these rates are lower, this can assist you in paying off all your outstanding debt.” ; Further noted many Namibians can now afford to buy a home because lower interest rates result in lower bond repayments ; “A phenomenon known as practical bias will result from this, whereby some of the group's items will see price increases that are higher than usual, while others won't. Practically speaking, the price of goods should fall in tandem with the rate of inflation Unfortunately, boosting competition is the only way to solve this problem.”

a1390.speaker: Alexander Ivanov, Director of the Officers' Commonwealth for International Security (SOMB)
a1390.speech: Said in an interview with TASS that the United States has lost ground in the Sahel because of its attitude toward the countries of the region: "That was the case in Niger when the United States decided that it could dictate to Niamey whom to cooperate with. But this only led the American military to leave the military bases in Niger. Thus, Washington lost its influence in the region and realised that it could not act in an authoritarian manner. Times have changed." ; He added that European leaders "are jealous of the Russian presence in the region and may even stage various provocations." "But for that, one must be prepared and learn to be independent and resilient in the face of external threats."

a1390.speaker: Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger (joint announcement of withdrawal from ECOWAS)
a1390.speech: On 28 January 2024 announced a joint decision to withdraw as quickly as possible from ECOWAS, which, according to them, "is under the influence of foreign powers, becoming a threat to the member states and their peoples."

a1390.speaker: Igor Gromyko, Russian Ambassador to Mali and Niger
a1390.speech: Said on 23 December that Russia intended to continue contributing to improving the combat capability of the national armed forces of the Sahel countries.

a1527.speaker: T.S., dismissed Afritextile employee
a1527.speech: Challenges management's explanations: "These are lies made up out of whole cloth." He says the cotton stock shortage invoked by the head of personnel is a tailor-made decision that in fact reveals the company leadership's agenda to reduce staff numbers ; according to him, the shortage was deliberately caused by the official in charge of supplies, who underestimated the company's needs, all the more so because warehouse managers had repeatedly reported the risk of a cotton stock shortage to their superiors, who did not react accordingly ; he points out that the head of personnel had declared in early July that the cotton stock shortage would be resolved by 15 July at the latest, but that to this day Afritextile has not bought a single gram of cotton.

a1527.speaker: P.K., Afritextile employee
a1527.speech: Fears that these "forced holidays" will lead to the closure of the company; insists that what worries them most today is that management continues to put other employees on leave and does not specify a return date: "It notifies the dismissed employees that they will be called back as soon as cotton is available." He indicates that management promised to pay employees on leave this month's salaries, but that if the shortage persists the company will not continue to pay them and will put them on technical unemployment, which could end in dismissal; he recalls that a cotton stock shortage was behind the company's closure in 2006.

a1527.speaker: S.C., dismissed Afritextile worker
a1527.speech: "The cotton stock shortage is linked to the poor management of the company. Those in charge of supplies ordered 800 tonnes when its needs were estimated at more than 1,200 tonnes of cotton." According to him it is incomprehensible that the shortage should occur in July, since it usually happens at the end of the year, the period when many employees take annual leave and technicians carry out machine maintenance ; he also deplores the absence of a safety stock at Afritextile, arguing that every company should have a minimum safety stock of three months, and urges the company's managers to diversify raw material suppliers: "National production is insufficient."

a1527.speaker: Félicien Niyonizigiye, Head of Personnel at Afritextile
a1527.speech: Reassures employees: "Let them rest assured. This is not a decision to close down or to lay off part of the staff. It is a simple company management measure." According to him there is nothing abnormal; such a measure often occurs when raw material stocks run out or during machine maintenance, generally at the end of the year. He explains the placing of certain employees on leave simply by the shortage of cotton, the basic raw material, and says there was no reason for spinning and weaving workshop staff to remain at the factory with nothing to do. He indicates that the company uses exclusively cotton supplied by the Cotton Management Company (Cogerco) and does not import it: "Importing is costly and takes at least three months." He reassures that workers on leave will receive their salaries at the end of the month and will be recalled as soon as Cogerco supplies cotton, its harvest campaign starting in two weeks.

a1527.speaker: Félicien Niyonizigiye, Head of Personnel at Afritextile
a1527.speech: Denies information circulated on social media referring to the closure of the factory: "Afritextile has no difficulties today that would push this company to reduce its staff," he hammers ; he also reassures customers: "There will be no shortage of fabrics and other Afritextile products. The company's activities are proceeding normally."

a1527.speaker: Pierre Claver Nahimana, Director General of Cogerco (Cotton Management Company)
a1527.speech: Indicates that national production cannot meet Afritextile's needs, Cogerco having produced about 800 tonnes of cotton last season whereas the needs of Burundi's textile industry are estimated at 1,200 tonnes ; says cotton production has declined in recent years, essentially for two reasons: the area given over to cotton growing has significantly decreased as the population has substituted food crops for cotton, and investment allocated to the crop has fallen ; testifies that in the past Burundi supplied the local textile industry and exported the surplus abroad, and regrets that today his company's production does not even meet local demand, recommending that the government invest more in this industrial crop.

a1547.speaker: Board of Directors of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a1547.speech: Approved a new Country Strategy Paper (CSP) worth 209 million dollars for Lesotho, establishing a roadmap to accelerate the transition towards economic diversification, resilience and inclusive growth.

a1547.speaker: Moono Mupotola, Deputy Director General for Southern Africa and Country Manager of the AfDB Group
a1547.speech: "Lesotho is at a decisive turning point" ; adding: "This comprehensive strategy draws on the country's abundant water resources, its strategic geographical location and its demographic dividend to open new paths towards inclusive growth and economic diversification."

a1547.speaker: Press release issued by APO Group on behalf of the AfDB
a1547.speech: States that the new CSP builds on the lessons learned from the Bank's previous operations in Lesotho and emphasises integrated, multi-sectoral approaches, better implementation capacity and proactive portfolio management, and that it is aligned with Lesotho's National Strategic Development Plan II (2018-2028), the AfDB's Ten-Year Strategy (2024-2033), the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

a1607.speaker: Tigray TV (regional television)
a1607.speech: Said on Sunday that three Ethiopian journalists investigating alleged illegal gold mines in the troubled Tigray region were abducted by unknown individuals before being released a few hours later; according to Tigray TV, the three men, who were not identified, were in the Asgede district when they were "abducted by unknown persons in unclear circumstances."

a1607.speaker: Abel Tsgabu, journalist with Tigray TV
a1607.speech: Told AFP a few hours later that they had been released and that they were "fine," without giving further details.

a1607.speaker: Olusegun Obasanjo, African Union envoy for the Horn of Africa
a1607.speech: Estimated that at least 600,000 people were killed during the war in Tigray.

a1757.speaker: Harriet Thompson, British High Commissioner to Ghana
a1757.speech: According to her, the expected growth in freight movement through Ghana's ports could be facilitated by the Prempeh I International Airport's operation coupled with existing partnerships between the two countries, and the Africa Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). She hoped to see the freight number go up with the commissioning of the Prempeh I International Airport. According to the UK High Commissioner in Ghana, the UK-Ghana partnership agreement as well as the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) will be instrumental in that increase.

a1757.speaker: Harriet Thompson, British High Commissioner to Ghana
a1757.speech: Reaffirmed the UK's commitment to supporting Ghana in promoting sustainable economic growth; emphasised the importance of collaboration between the UK and Ghana in fostering trade and infrastructure development; underscored the UK's reputation in construction, emphasising the quality of infrastructure that British companies build, known for durability and longevity; and emphasised the partnership approach, where British companies collaborate with local firms, sharing expertise and contributing to local development.

a2005.speaker: Jenfan Muswere, Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services Minister
a2005.speech: Speaking at a post-Cabinet media briefing on Tuesday, said the government had approved the venue for the 2026 celebrations and taken stock of legacy projects associated with previous hosts ; “The selection of Matabeleland South is not only symbolic, but strategic. Maphisa carries deep historical resonance in Zimbabwe’s liberation history. The event will drive inclusive development through significant infrastructure investments in the province.”

a2005.speaker: Jenfan Muswere, Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services Minister
a2005.speech: Said the Maphisa event is expected to unlock economic growth opportunities through improved connectivity and service delivery in Matabeleland South through key initiatives including the rehabilitation of the Bulawayo-Maphisa and Gwanda-Maphisa roads, as well as a strategic extension of the Bulawayo-Maphisa Road to Mpoengs at the Botswana border, aimed at strengthening regional trade links and social cohesion ; “The hosting model has proven that national celebrations can be more than symbolic, they are a tool for tangible development. These legacy projects are transforming the face of our provinces.”

a2005.speaker: Jenfan Muswere, Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services Minister
a2005.speech: Reaffirmed Government’s commitment to ensuring that all provinces benefit equitably through rotational hosting, and that each Independence Day celebration leaves a footprint of progress ; “Each province will get its turn, and with that turn, comes a permanent improvement in infrastructure and community welfare.”

a2005.speaker: Cabinet of Zimbabwe (Cabinet resolutions)
a2005.speech: According to Cabinet resolutions, a US$32.5 million budget has been approved to complete ongoing legacy projects in the Midlands province, which hosted the commemorations this year.

a2005.speaker: Cabinet of Zimbabwe
a2005.speech: Cabinet noted that US$2.5 million has been set aside to complete outstanding development works in Manicaland and Mashonaland Central, both of which previously hosted the national event.

a2089.speaker: Minister(s) of International Affairs and Cooperation and of the Interior of Mozambique
a2089.speech: In these engagements, the Executive Secretary was informed of the relative stability that has returned to Cabo Delgado province due to the combined efforts of the Rapid Deployment Capability of the SADC Standby Force (RDC SSF), Forcas Armadas de Defesa de Mocambique (FADM) and the Rwanda Security Forces.

a2089.speaker: Secretary of the Province of Cabo Delgado
a2089.speech: Informed him that the good work of SAMIM has restored stability and some of the IDPs were returning to their homes.

a2089.speaker: Major General Xolani Mankayi, SAMIM Force Commander
a2089.speech: Briefed the Executive Secretary on the progress made by the RDC SSF since its deployment in July 2021.

a2089.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a2089.speech: In his address, commended SAMIM forces for their professional conduct in executing their mandate in Mozambique; apprised them of the high accolades from International Cooperating partners and the Government of the Republic of Mozambique of their professional conduct and urged them to continue being a beacon of hope for the people of Cabo Delgado Province and Mozambique in the fight against terrorism; pledged utmost support to the Force Commander and that the SADC region will ensure the success of SAMIM.

a2089.speaker: General Joaquim Rivas Mangrasse, Chief of General Staff of FADM, and Major General Mpho Mophuting, Deputy Commander, Botswana Defence Force
a2089.speech: The two Generals appreciated the conditions the troops were facing against the terrorists and urged SAMIM forces to do their best and make the region proud by degrading the terrorists and stabilising the Cabo Delgado Province with the ultimate goal of achieving peace in Mozambique and the region.

a2089.speaker: SADC Mission in Mozambique (SAMIM) (media release)
a2089.speech: "SAMIM would like to assure the people of Mozambique and SADC of a collective commitment to achieving a peaceful, stable and secure Cabo Delgado as well as the entire country of Mozambique."

a2512.speaker: Ntsokoane Matekane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a2512.speech: Has made an ambitious pledge to create 70 000 jobs for unemployed youth within just a month.

a2512.speaker: ILO statistics
a2512.speech: Lesotho's unemployment rate stands at 16.15 percent, with youth unemployment even higher, according to ILO statistics.

a2512.speaker: Dr Retselisitsoe Matlanyane, Finance Minister of Lesotho
a2512.speech: Presented concerns over youth unemployment in the country at the beginning of the year, which she said has left scores between 15 and 35 disheartened; Matlanyane said an estimated 760 000 young people were unemployed while only 145 000 were employed.

a2517.speaker: 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS)
a2517.speech: has shown that more Nigerian women than men have been diagnosed and treated for hypertension; the survey shows that 52 per cent of women have ever had their blood pressure measured by a doctor or other health care worker, compared to 32 per cent of men, and that among those tested, eight per cent of women and five per cent of men reported being told by a health professional that they have high blood pressure or hypertension ; The report further reveals that among women diagnosed with hypertension in the past 12 months, 72 per cent were prescribed medication to control their blood pressure, while 54 per cent were currently taking the prescribed medication; among men diagnosed in the same period, 69 per cent were prescribed medication, and 51 per cent reported taking it.

a2517.speaker: Second Global Hypertension Report (WHO, Bloomberg Philanthropies and Resolve to Save Lives)
a2517.speech: The 2024 report revealed that 1.4 billion people worldwide were living with hypertension, highlighting the urgent need for stronger global action on prevention and treatment ; the global report called on governments to strengthen national hypertension control programmes and ensure equitable access to care.

a2517.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a2517.speech: According to WHO, only 28 per cent of low-income countries have all WHO-recommended hypertension medicines readily available in pharmacies or primary health facilities. This contrasts 93 per cent of high-income countries, highlighting the inequality in access to essential treatment.

a2517.speaker: Nigerian Hypertension Society (NHS)
a2517.speech: warned that treatment coverage remains alarmingly low.

a2517.speaker: Simeon Isezuo, President of the Nigerian Hypertension Society
a2517.speech: In a statement marking World Hypertension Day in May, disclosed that only about 10 per cent of Nigerians living with hypertension are currently receiving treatment for the condition.

a2517.speaker: Nigerian government
a2517.speech: In June 2025, the Nigerian government raised concerns that many cases of hypertension in the country remain undiagnosed, adding to the country's rising burden of non-communicable diseases.

a2517.speaker: Salma Anas, Special Adviser to the President on Health
a2517.speech: Speaking at the 25th Annual Scientific Conference and General Meetings of the Nigerian Hypertension Society in Abuja, noted that “nearly one in three Nigerian adults has hypertension, yet many are unaware of their condition.”

a2532.speaker: Samson Mndolo, Malawi Secretary for Health
a2532.speech: Said that in the unpredictable HIV financing realities, there is a demand for more efficiency and resilience. "We must achieve better health outcomes with the limited resources available. It is extremely difficult to secure additional funding for health. We must explore practical models for maintaining and expanding services for key and vulnerable populations within constrained funding environments and develop shared priorities for national action and regional collaboration to ensure a sustainable and resilient HIV response," he said.

a2532.speaker: Samson Mndolo, Malawi Secretary for Health
a2532.speech: He added that national leaders, policymakers, programme implementers and partners must recognise that the decisions they make today will shape the future of the HIV response ; Mndolo also said that the time has come for broad action, where stakeholders must move beyond dialogue to implementation, ensuring that strategies are not only responsive to today's funding realities but also contribute to stronger, more integrated health systems.

a2532.speaker: Linley Chewere, Director for HIV, Aids, STIs and Viral Hepatitis at Malawi's Ministry of Health
a2532.speech: Said that following the suspension of US support, the government had to quickly step in to prevent interruptions. Chewere added that with Malawi's HIV response having been largely donor-dependent, with the government contributing just about 20 percent, the funding cuts prompted the immediate development of a minimum package of services. "Based on staffing levels, existing evidence, cost-effectiveness and sustainability, we identified interventions the government could offer with or without donor support. This is now what we are implementing," she said.

a2532.speaker: Linley Chewere, Director for HIV, Aids, STIs and Viral Hepatitis at Malawi's Ministry of Health
a2532.speech: Chewere added that government-employed health workers took over from partners who had been operating in several health facilities. "The response is now government-led; the government sets the direction for HIV efforts. Additionally, our health and HIV information systems were previously partner-led. We are now working to establish government-led systems. We are currently assessing all existing systems in the country," she said.

a2532.speaker: Linley Chewere, Director for HIV, Aids, STIs and Viral Hepatitis at Malawi's Ministry of Health
a2532.speech: The Ministry of Health official further told the gathering that the government has also increased funding for the HIV response, including for antiretroviral therapy ; She added that the government is also reviewing the role of implementing partners, so that they do not deliver services directly, but offer technical assistance.

a2532.speaker: Charles Holmes, Centre for Innovation in Global Health at Georgetown University
a2532.speech: Noted that governments and civil society are finding ways to safeguard key programmes amid funding uncertainty. He added that the stakeholders are preparing for progressive acts such as the scale-up of a long-acting HIV prevention drug, which has since been backed by the World Health Organisation. "These efforts are aligned with UNAids' vital work on sustainability roadmaps, which will be an important driver of long-term epidemic control," Holmes said.

a2550.speaker: Nkhotakota District Health Office
a2550.speech: Says malaria affects over 80 percent of the district's population and called for urgent action to curb the spread of the disease.

a2550.speaker: Jacob Kafulafula, Nkhotakota district health director
a2550.speech: Said they will distribute insecticide-treated nets as part of efforts to implement the national malaria prevention and treatment policy: “Malaria remains a significant health challenge in Nkhotakota where for every 1 000 people, 823 are affected. This underscores the urgent need for effective interventions.” ; “The district has previously employed indoor-residual spraying as a preventive measure. However, the distribution of nets is seen as a crucial additional step.”

a2550.speaker: Willard Magunda, Nkhotakota district principal education officer (speaking on behalf of district commissioner Ben Tohno)
a2550.speech: Expressed optimism about the impact of sleeping under the nets and urged the community to use the nets correctly and not for other purposes such as fishing: “It is disheartening to see that people misuse the nets. We need everyone's cooperation to ensure the initiative achieves its goal of reducing malaria cases in the district.”

a2550.speaker: Madalitso Kafelemu, beneficiary
a2550.speech: Welcomed the initiative: “I will urge members of my family to sleep under the nets. Malaria is one of the deadly diseases.”

a2587.speaker: Civil society organizations and opposition parties
a2587.speech: have intensified calls for the resignations of MERA CEO Henry Kachaje and Minister of Energy Ibrahim Matola, accusing them of negligence and mismanagement, and contending that both officials failed to ensure proper fuel procurement and management systems, despite clear warnings of impending shortages.

a2587.speaker: Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC)
a2587.speech: have warned of nationwide protests if these officials do not step down.

a2648.speaker: Pamela Kuwali, CARE Malawi Country Director
a2648.speech: Has declared that Malawi has the potential to achieve national food self-sufficiency, following the successful implementation of community-led irrigation schemes under the USAID-funded Titukulane project ; Highlighting success stories, noted farmers like Anifa, who turned a MWK 300,000 ($176) investment into projected earnings of MWK 1.2 million ($706) from beans, and Mr. Maulidi, who purchased a motorcycle worth MWK 3.2 million ($2,000) from his harvest profits: “These are stories of dignity and transformation. What moved me most was the pride in the eyes of the farmers, especially the women, leading change in their households.” ; “We have the land, the water, and the will. Now we need bold leadership and action, because food security is not a dream, it’s a decision.”

a2648.speaker: Sam Kawale, Minister of Agriculture
a2648.speech: Who officially commissioned the scheme, praised the project as a model for climate resilience and agricultural progress: “Irrigation is no longer a luxury, it’s a necessity,” he said, adding that the initiative supports Malawi’s Vision 2063, which aims to commercialise agriculture and boost productivity through sustainable technologies ; Also commended CARE Malawi’s engagement of local artisans in constructing the schemes, enhancing sustainability and community ownership, and emphasised the government’s collaboration with financial institutions such as NEEF and COFI to help farmers access input loans and expand production.

a2663.speaker: Political charter of the “Founding Alliance of Sudan” signed by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and 23 political-military groups (document cited by international press)
a2663.speech: In the political charter, the paramilitary and political groups agree on principles and foundations for the construction of a new nation, one that would be a secular and democratic State, based on a principle of voluntary and decentralised unity. In the charter, cited by the international press, the groups state that they want the new government in the areas controlled by the paramilitaries, such as western Darfur and parts of Kordofan, to be based on freedom, equality, justice and respect for diversity. The document does not specify where the seat of government would be, but states that its objective will be to end the war and guarantee unobstructed access to humanitarian aid.

a2663.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and their partners (non-response)
a2663.speech: The signing of this agreement took place this Saturday in the Kenyan capital, after months of talks between the parties involved, without the paramilitaries and their partners having made any declaration on the meaning of this document in the short term.

a2663.speaker: United Civil Forces (broad coalition of political parties, civil society representatives and armed factions)
a2663.speech: Also confirmed the signing to Agence France Presse.

a2768.speaker: Davies Narh Korboe, President of the Federation of Associations of Ghanaian Exporters (FAGE)
a2768.speech: "The Ghana Horticulture Expo is not just an event - it is a vision materialized. It reflects our deep resolve to transition Ghana from a raw produce exporter into a value-added, globally competitive horticulture powerhouse." ; "We are not only showcasing our fruits, vegetables, tubers, and herbs. We are showcasing the future of Ghana's economy - one that is inclusive, sustainable and export-ready, operating around the clock."

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On the meaning of the 18 December 1958 proclamation of the Republic of Niger: said that to explain a historical fact one must put it back in its context, and that 18 December cannot have the same connotation for Nigeriens today as for those living in 1958. Historically 18 December appears as a break with the earlier situation in which the colonial administration ran the country and Nigeriens were all considered subjects, "a very polite way of treating people as slaves", with no rights and no recourse; the population owned nothing and people did not have the status of citizens on their own territory. Said colonisation lasted some fifty years in Niger, a very short period that nonetheless destroyed everything in the way populations managed their countries, their relations, trade and communication routes, and that its gravest achievement was making Africans accept that they were inferior in every field, despite civilisations as old as Koumbi Saleh, the Mali empire, Songhai and Kanem. Said the birth of the Republic gave rise to the hope of building their own Republic and taking their own decisions, and that compared with the situation of 1958 it was "a giant step", welcomed with enormous joy.

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On post-proclamation division and colonial influence: said one of the major drawbacks was that most leaders who had initially come together within the same political structure found themselves divided, and that the RDA-SAWABA opposition tarnished the joy Nigeriens might have had. Said the proclamation of the Republic is different from independence, consisting of a sort of autonomy; said the oppositions among Nigeriens arose precisely because colonial influence "was real and manifest", that pressure exerted to bring people to accept the French Community was also a reality, that some people have even spoken of election rigging, and that perhaps one day historians will come back with detail to say exactly what happened.

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On whether post-national-conference political actors served the Republic: said that in history one avoids value judgements and places things in context; recalled 15 years of RDA rule and 13 years of the CMS, a first regime that established a single party holding a monopoly on national reflection, justified at the time by the belief that democratic pluralism would provoke splits, and a second regime, a "praetorian autocracy" under Kountche, in which no political party functioned and no political demonstration was authorised. Said Niger therefore arrived at the National Conference without any practice of democracy. Said democracy is expensive and that, as the pioneers of democracy began their functions, "the West, as usual, took steps to ensure that the funds and support we received changed in nature"; said France decided to devote all its efforts to uranium to the detriment of the local economy, that the aid granted was subject to conditionalities that do not favour intervention, and that on the international level the same partners chose that period to devalue all Niger's export products and create a financial shortfall. Said the people themselves did not have a "democratic" political consciousness and that elections became a competition between ethnic groups or regions; concluded that he speaks not of failures but of shortcomings in the construction of a democratic Republic in Niger.

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On the values to capitalise on as achievements of the Republic: said that after the events of 26 July 2023, when ECOWAS announced a plan for military aggression, Nigeriens mobilised to stand behind the CNSP, and that even Nigeriens who disagreed with the coup or belonged to the party that had lost power were not in favour of a military intervention on Nigerien soil. Said this is an achievement of the Republic, the consciousness of belonging to a single entity and the will to defend it at the cost of one's life; recalled that in 1958 there was no Nigerien nation but independent principalities, traditional chieftaincies and sultanates that had to be brought to accept the authority of a single State. Said "We are on the way to constituting a nation. Loyalty to the Republic is a reality."

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On consolidating that achievement: said the first thing is to train citizens - "The civic and political education of a people is indispensable if one wants to create a strong and respected nation" - and that when a citizen is fully aware of his rights, duties and obligations the country gains ten years. Said the State must give the population the means to appraise the political acts it takes; said that in politics the acts committed today precede you by 50 years and that any act committing the country's future must be agreed and accepted by the majority of the people, the only way to ensure the durability of a regime. Said the role of civil society organisations is a priority because civil society is in direct and permanent contact with the population and must be the receptacle of its needs and the vector transmitting its wishes and demands to the authorities - a role that is not political but one of guiding, training and raising the awareness of citizens.

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On political parties failing to provide civic training: said this is one of the pitfalls of a generation that frankly lacked the necessary political culture, but that people were extremely courageous; said he was part of that generation, which had no practical political training and spent nearly 30 years without any possibility of political activity, unlike today's young people with their fada. Said a country is not built solely with popular measures and that unpopular measures can bear fruit in the future, which is why citizens need the capacity to analyse such actions. Said the parties did not take on civic training because it has a cost and the parties born at that time had little; said intellectuals and senior cadres capable of understanding democracy abandoned or were excluded from the National Assembly over successive elections because they had only their salary, and were replaced by traders and "hunters of public contracts" with no mastery of democracy or politics. Said one cannot say everything done was a failure, recalling that when he began working in 1970 he doubted there were 20 degree-holders in all of Niger: "How do you build a country in those conditions? But they did their best."

a2945.speaker: Kalla Karimoune, historian and former diplomat
a2945.speech: On the refoundation of the State and the creation of the AES: said he was one of the very first to insist on the rapprochement between the three countries because they live through the same problems and have had the same adversaries, and that pooling efforts, means and intelligence could help face these challenges. Said being in the AES is an excellent thing but the greatest benefit cannot be drawn from it without a stable, organised State unanimously supported by the population; said the first quality of a power is its attentiveness to the people and that leaders must explain their choices, "because if you do not explain to the people, it is rumour that will take control of the street". Said the three AES leaders must remain in harmony with their populations and respect their aspirations; called for social justice - the same punishment for the same fault and the same rewards for the same efforts - and for African leaders to respect their peoples, since the people are the only entity capable of defending them. Contrasted the Western conception of power with traditional Djerma chieftaincy practice, said that in certain African societies a leader who distinguished himself by cruelty or poor management is erased from the genealogy of power, and that banishment from the community is not a new phenomenon. Concluded that in just 50 years colonisation destroyed thousand-year-old values and that "We must return to our values and build our nations on the basis of our history, our values and according to our aspirations."

a3008.speaker: Pamela Fessenden, United States Charge d'Affaires in Malawi
a3008.speech: Has said Malawi has, through the establishment of the Asset Forfeiture Unit, seized $150,000 (about K267 million) of illicit funds and frozen assets worth $3 million (K5.8 billion) related to corruption ; "The newly established Asset Forfeiture Unit has played a pivotal role in identifying and recovering proceeds from graft, marking a significant milestone in the country's ongoing battle against corruption. The strategy emphasises a multi-stakeholder approach, aligning efforts from local institutions and international partners" ; said such efforts were part of a coordinated anti-corruption strategy developed with support from the United States Agency for International Development (Usaid) and partners from the United Kingdom.

a3008.speaker: Willy Kambwandira, Executive Director of the Centre for Social Accountability and Transparency (CSAT)
a3008.speech: Said although there had been notable gains, such as increased awareness and institutional reforms, there were persistent setbacks that highlighted the ongoing struggle to achieve meaningful and lasting change ; "Gains have been achieved in the fight against corruption. However, the pace of reform and enforcement remains inconsistent" ; said establishing dedicated courts to handle corruption-related crimes by the government was ensuring that justice was delivered in a timely manner, but pointed out that despite the establishment of specialised courts, many corruption cases experienced prolonged delays, undermining public trust in the justice system.

a3008.speaker: Elyvin Nkhonjera Chawinga, mining expert
a3008.speech: Underscored the need for stronger advocacy and collective action to hold authorities accountable and sustain the momentum in combating corruption ; "While Malawi has taken important steps to address corruption, significant challenges remained. The journey towards a corruption-free society requires continuous effort, stronger institutional commitment and greater public participation" ; lamented information gaps on mining issues: "Limited disclosure of mining contracts, revenue and environmental assessments discourage investments and affect public trust."

a3008.speaker: Rebecca Hami, youths representative
a3008.speech: Said there was a need for individuals to be discussing corruption issues openly ; "Corruption remains a significant challenge, with many discussions but little concrete action being taken to address it effectively."

a3037.speaker: Gugu, 54-year-old HIV-positive former sex worker and patient of a USAID-funded clinic in Johannesburg
a3037.speech: “I was one of the people who was able to get their medication in bulk. I usually collect a three-month prescription. But before my clinic closed, they gave me nine months' worth of medication.”

a3187.speaker: Josephine Achol, 26-year-old Nutrition Assistant with Amref in Tonj, Warrap State
a3187.speech: "Finding a job in Juba was difficult, so I returned to Tonj, determined to put my knowledge into practice." ; "I started in the Stabilization Center at the Hospital in Tonj South, where I learned how to prepare Therapeutic Milk for malnourished children. A nurse named Regina mentored me, teaching me the essentials of nutrition and care." ; "My dedication did not go unnoticed. Staff from Amref saw my commitment and encouraged me. Even though I wasn't earning a salary, I continued volunteering for six months because I found fulfillment in the work that I did for my community." ; "My colleagues noticed my struggle, and on their own initiative, they would contribute small amounts to help me with transport and my basic needs. It was a difficult time, but their support kept me going."

a3187.speaker: Josephine Achol, 26-year-old Nutrition Assistant with Amref in Tonj, Warrap State
a3187.speech: "I was nervous but applied, trusting wholeheartedly in my faith" ; "When I received the call from HR informing me that I had been selected as a Nutrition Assistant, I couldn't believe it. I remember a time when I prayed for just a small paid opportunity - anything that could earn me even $50." ; "When I received my first salary, it was beyond what I had imagined. My colleagues laughed at how shocked I was. That moment marked the beginning of a new chapter in my life."

a3187.speaker: Josephine Achol, 26-year-old Nutrition Assistant with Amref in Tonj, Warrap State
a3187.speech: "Many parents wait until a child is critically ill before seeking help. After education, I conduct screenings to identify cases of moderate and severe acute malnutrition (SAM)." ; "I also screen pregnant and lactating mothers to assess their nutritional needs. We are two Nutrition Assistants at the facility, so we divide tasks - one screens while the other handles treatment and distribution of supplies, assisted by two Community Nutrition Volunteers (CNVs)."

a3187.speaker: Josephine Achol, 26-year-old Nutrition Assistant with Amref in Tonj, Warrap State
a3187.speech: "One of the most memorable cases I've handled was a 10-month-old child from Tonj who was severely malnourished. At first, I wasn't sure if the child would survive" ; "For a full year, we treated this child, and despite the challenges we faced, she fully recovered. Seeing that child healthy again reminded me why this work is so important - why I did it in the first place."

a3187.speaker: Josephine Achol, 26-year-old Nutrition Assistant with Amref in Tonj, Warrap State
a3187.speech: Says many families wrongly believe malnutrition is a spiritual matter, and seek help from herbalists instead of professional medical care; said such misconceptions and cultural beliefs are a particular challenge, as families only realized that the patient needs medical attention when their situation is already critical ; "There were many misconceptions in the community about malnutrition. Families were used to eating only one type of food. Through continuous health education, we have helped change mindsets, and more families now understand the importance of balanced nutrition."

a3187.speaker: Josephine Achol, 26-year-old Nutrition Assistant with Amref in Tonj, Warrap State
a3187.speech: Said communities in Tonj are learning about good feeding and changing their lives thanks to the nutrition project of WFP and Unicef through Amref Health Africa in South Sudan ; "With recent budget cuts from USAID, the challenges have increased. However, I am determined to find a way - I run a small shop in town and plan to start a vegetable garden to raise funds for my studies." ; "I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to work in this field. Despite the hardships, I know that every child we help, every mother we educate, and every life we save is a step toward a healthier community."

a3359.speaker: Over 3,000 former Malawian employees of Project Hope Namibia-Malawi (PHN-MW)
a3359.speech: Are demanding justice after being unlawfully and brutally cast aside despite a clear directive from the United States Government not to terminate contracts, calling the conduct "blatant discrimination, abuse of power, and financial injustice." ; Say PHN-MW hasn't remitted pension contributions since December 2024, further deepening their sense of betrayal and financial ruin.

a3359.speaker: Former PHN-MW employees (collective demands)
a3359.speech: Are calling for urgent intervention from USAID and the US Embassy, Malawi Labour Authorities and Independent Auditors, demanding immediate payment of all outstanding salaries and benefits, reinstatement of contracts now that the project is back, and a full investigation into PHN-MW's financial management and ethical conduct.

a3359.speaker: One dismissed PHN-MW staff member (anonymous)
a3359.speech: "They said there was no money to pay us—but somehow, they're still drawing massive salaries while we can't even buy food for our families," one dismissed staff member told Nyasa Times.

a3359.speaker: One former PHN-MW employee (anonymous)
a3359.speech: "Where is the justice?" cried one former employee. "We were tossed out like garbage, left to starve, while top executives keep cashing in. Is this what USAID stands for?"

a3359.speaker: United States Government (USG) stop work order, January 2025
a3359.speech: Issued a "stop work" order, temporarily pausing project activities pending a review; importantly, the order did not authorize contract terminations.

a3359.speaker: United States Government (USG), March 24, 2025
a3359.speech: Lifted the suspension and authorized all implementing partners to resume work.

a3359.speaker: Project Hope Namibia-Malawi (PHN-MW) management
a3359.speech: Axed over 3,000 employees within a mere seven days, citing lack of funds ; promised to pay workers up to March 10th ; told former employees they must reapply for their jobs, despite being unlawfully dismissed in the first place.

a3359.speaker: Dr. Endale, PHN-MW's Chief of Party
a3359.speech: Attempts to reach him were unsuccessful. He did not respond to calls or messages, fueling further frustration among former employees.

a3715.speaker: JD Vance, US Vice-President
a3715.speech: Urged European leaders to drop the 'firewalls' they have erected to keep far-right parties out of government ; ‘The threat that I worry most about, vis-a-vis Europe, is not Russia, it’s not China, it’s not any other external actor.’ ; ‘What I worry about is the threat from within: the retreat of Europe from some of its most fundamental values – values shared with the United States of America.’

a3715.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3715.speech: Said Ukraine was responsible for starting the war and branded its President Volodymyr Zelensky a ‘dictator.’

a3715.speaker: Pete Hegseth, US Defence Secretary
a3715.speech: Shocked Europe by warning them not to assume the US would defend them ‘forever.’

a3715.speaker: Pete Hegseth, US Defence Secretary
a3715.speech: Reportedly said AFRICOM’s role remained vital to US interests ; cited the 1 February airstrikes against militants in Somalia that AFRICOM coordinated with the Federal Government of Somalia ; also said Africa remained a priority because of China’s ‘pernicious’ intentions on the continent.

a3715.speaker: Priyal Singh, ISS Senior Researcher
a3715.speech: Saw ‘a breakdown in the transatlantic partnership,’ believing the traditional assumption that there was a unified collective ‘West’ ‘doesn’t hold true anymore’ ; said Africa’s relations with Europe would probably stay on the same path – of good governance, human rights and so on – but its relationship with the US would likely go down a very different path ; added that after Mr Vance told Europe it would henceforth have to take care of its own security, this raised questions about the US approach to security in Africa ; said it’s unclear whether Europe could fill the security gap left in Africa by the US, as it would have to increase defence spending on Ukraine to compensate for an expected drop in US military support.

a3715.speaker: Jim Risch, US Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman
a3715.speech: Said that ‘UN Security Council Resolution 2719 should not be used to fund AUSSOM. Doing so would lock the US into perpetual funding through its dues to the UN which is a disservice to the American taxpayer.’

a3715.speaker: Jakkie Cilliers, head of ISS’ International Futures programme
a3715.speech: Said the past week’s events were ‘hopefully … a wake-up call for Europe’ to ‘get serious about taking responsibility for your own security’ ; said the US and Europe’s diverging paths would impact Africa mainly through Mr Trump’s decision to slash foreign aid and the inability of Europe to bridge that gap, leading to a dramatic increase in poverty from an expected 20 to 30 per cent cut in US aid for fighting HIV/AIDS and development, so that the US’ image as a reliable partner would give way to a sense that it is ‘fickle and unpredictable,’ losing considerable soft power ; said AFRICOM remained vital because Africa was on the front lines of an attack by Islamists against Christian populations.

a3715.speaker: Ottilia Anna Maunganidze, ISS Head of Special Projects
a3715.speech: Noted that after Vance left the Munich conference, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi took the stage and emphasised many of the things Mr Vance hadn’t mentioned ; ‘It was a message that resonated with many people, which was ironic because traditionally China has been the outsider in these discussions. Yet in this case … his was the one that got the standing ovation that JD Vance’s didn’t get.’ ; thought the juxtaposition of Mr Vance’s hostile speech and Yi ‘basically reaffirming a global order based on mutually agreed rules’ sent the message – also to Africa – that ‘if the US doesn’t want to be a world leader … we’re happy to do that by pushing a development agenda’ ; said China’s approach of security via development would have especially appealed to Africa.

a3715.speaker: Wang Yi, Chinese Foreign Minister
a3715.speech: Emphasised multilateralism, collaborating for development and building stronger partnerships.

a3877.speaker: New global study published in The Lancet
a3877.speech: Suggests that progress in vaccinating children against a variety of life-threatening diseases has stalled in the past two decades – and even gone backwards in some countries; says measles vaccinations have declined in nearly 100 countries; researchers say vaccine coverage doubled in nearly half a century until 2023, but since 2010 progress has stagnated; by 2023, there were nearly 16 million children who had not had any childhood vaccinations – most of them in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

a3877.speaker: The researchers (study authors)
a3877.speech: Are calling for a concerted effort to provide better and more equal access to vaccines; recommend that all countries try to strengthen primary healthcare systems and combat misinformation around vaccines to prevent parents being hesitant about getting their children vaccinated.

a3877.speaker: The report's authors
a3877.speech: Warn that vaccination rates have fallen in Europe, the US and other wealthy countries too.

a3877.speaker: Child health experts
a3877.speech: Warn that cuts to international aid budgets that fund vaccination programmes, combined with vaccine scepticism, are creating a “perfect storm”.

a3877.speaker: Dr Jonathan Mosser, study author, Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington
a3877.speech: Says large numbers of children remain under-vaccinated and un-vaccinated. “Routine childhood vaccinations are among the most powerful and cost-effective public health interventions available, but persistent global inequalities, challenges from the Covid pandemic, and the growth of vaccine misinformation and hesitancy have all contributed to faltering immunisation progress,” he said ; said there was now an increased risk of outbreaks of diseases like measles, polio and diphtheria, and that all children should benefit from life-saving immunisations.

a3877.speaker: Professor Sir Andrew Pollard, director of the Oxford Vaccine Group
a3877.speech: Says the findings present a concerning picture. “More children will be hospitalised, permanently damaged and die from fully preventable diseases if the trend is not reversed. Alas, the cuts in global health funding mean that this situation is set to deteriorate.”

a3877.speaker: Dr David Elliman, University College London
a3877.speech: Says many factors have contributed to the current situation. “Around the world, the increasing number of countries torn apart by civil unrest and wars, combined with the drastic cuts in foreign aid from rich nations, such as USA and UK, makes it difficult to get vaccines to many populations,” he said. “Where it appears that policy is being made on the basis of ill-informed opinion, rather than science, we have a perfect storm.”

a3916.speaker: IOM Director General (IOM Chief), speaking live from Port Sudan
a3916.speech: "The situation here in Sudan is catastrophic. There is simply no other way to put it. Hunger, disease and sexual violence are rampant. For the people of Sudan, this is a living nightmare." ; "This is an underreported conflict situation, and we must pay it more attention. Millions are suffering, and there is now the serious possibility of the conflict igniting regional instability from the Sahel to the Horn of Africa to the Red Sea." ; said she arrived on a four-day visit into a deteriorating security situation with alarming reports of new atrocities, and had heard distressing detail from teams on the ground.

a3916.speaker: IOM Director General (IOM Chief), speaking live from Port Sudan
a3916.speech: "Today I can share that we will release new figures this week showing the displacement number has hit 11 million. That's up 200,000 just since September." ; said another 3.1 million people have travelled across borders to flee the fighting, that in total nearly 30 per cent of Sudan's population has been displaced, that more than half of those displaced are women and more than a quarter of them children under the age of five, and that Sudan has been the world's largest displacement crisis throughout this year.

a3916.speaker: IOM Director General (IOM Chief), speaking live from Port Sudan
a3916.speech: Said one in every two Sudanese is struggling to get even the minimal amount of food to survive, that famine conditions have taken hold in North Darfur, and described visiting the Arbaat dam area about 40 kilometres from Port Sudan where a spillway collapsed after heavy rains in August, with the resulting flood killing at least 148 people and devastating homes, livestock and infrastructure.

a3916.speaker: IOM Director General (IOM Chief), speaking live from Port Sudan
a3916.speech: "The parties to this conflict must do what they have pledged to do – and what international humanitarian law requires – protect civilians, and ensure safe, swift and unimpeded access to life-saving assistance." ; said the safety of aid workers is often threatened and access restrictions and bureaucratic impediments continue to be imposed, and that "People are dying because of this."

a3916.speaker: IOM Director General (IOM Chief), speaking live from Port Sudan
a3916.speech: "Sudan is easily the most neglected crisis in the world today. The collective failure to act means the devastation risks spilling over into neighboring countries." ; said that at a conference in Paris this past April the international community made generous pledges but that appeal is only 52 per cent funded, and that although IOM has been able to help nearly 3 million people since the war started, IOM's part of the response plan is only 20 per cent funded ; "The humanitarian response must be scaled up, and we call on the donor community to support this effort." ; echoed the Secretary General in calling for an end to hostilities, protection for civilians, and access for humanitarian agencies so that aid can flow ; "We will not allow Sudan to be forgotten. But its people need peace, now."

a3916.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a3916.speech: Shone the spotlight on this suffering yesterday, calling it an ‘utter humanitarian catastrophe’, and reported yesterday that almost 25 million people are now requiring assistance.

a3925.speaker: Maria Price Detherage, USAID Senior Official in charge of Southern Africa
a3925.speech: “Partnering to support democratic governance is a top priority for the U.S. Government,” said Detherage during the launch ceremony. “USAID believes and invests in the power of local governance. In partnership with the Government of Mozambique and in support of the national decentralization agenda, the expansion of the LOGOS program offers an opportunity to improve the delivery of basic services, such as health, education, water, and sanitation, as well as increase transparency and accountability to citizens.”

a3949.speaker: Naledi Pandor, South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation
a3949.speech: Says South Africa will not turn its back on Cuba and told Parliament on Thursday it would be unethical for South Africa to turn a blind eye to Cuba’s economic situation, reiterating the government’s support of Cuba in her department’s budget vote: “Many countries ask for assistance. We will continue to contribute what we can. We believe this is a vital obligation, and as one of the world’s nations, we must honour it. We are also prepared to act in solidarity with our brothers and sisters in Cuba. As we cannot turn a blind eye to their plight while their economy is strangled by illegal blockades and sanctions. The Cuban economy has been brought to its knees after 61 years of draconian US sanctions imposed on the impoverished island nation.”

a3949.speaker: Naledi Pandor, South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation
a3949.speech: Previously said Cuba faced chronic food, fuel, medicine and electricity shortages.

a3949.speaker: Naledi Pandor, South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation
a3949.speech: Said Cuba’s assistance to South Africa during apartheid could not be underestimated: “This is a nation that stood shoulder to shoulder with our combatants in the struggle for freedom. And we must help if we can. It was the Cubans who sent their sons and daughters to fight for the liberation of southern Africa. Of course those who were never in the trenches fighting for freedom cannot appreciate this history. Cuba played a pivotal role in turning the tide against our colonial oppressors. It would be unjustified and unethical to turn our backs on them in their hour of greatest need. We will also consolidate the causes of other countries.”

a3949.speaker: Gauteng High Court in Pretoria (ruling)
a3949.speech: Dismissed, with costs, the government’s application for leave to appeal the court’s ruling that AfriForum could interdict it from donating R50 million to Cuba.

a3949.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President
a3949.speech: Said health items, and not money, would be donated to Cuba.

a3949.speaker: News24 (March report)
a3949.speech: Reported that the government had no plans to write off an R84.6 million loan made to the Cuban government in 2021.

a3949.speaker: Department of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa (@DIRCO_ZA, social media post, May 11 2022)
a3949.speech: “The Department of International Relations and Cooperation of the Republic of South Africa condemns in the strongest possible terms the killing of Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh allegedly by the Israeli Defence Force on Wednesday 11 May 2022.”

a3949.speaker: Supra Mahumapelo, ANC MP and chairperson of Parliament’s International Relations Committee
a3949.speech: Said the matter should be dealt with in line with the Constitution and South Africa’s historical relationship with Cuba: “Look at the implications of the court judgment. It is our expectation that the department will report and account to Parliament on this matter. We will ensure that the department focuses its energies on economic diplomacy.”

a3949.speaker: Mkhuleko Hlengwa, IFP MP
a3949.speech: Said South Africa must continue to make its presence known on the international stage, and highlighted the department’s poor financial management: “The department incurred unauthorised expenditure of R150 million. The irregular expenditure was R187 million. There are serious questions to be asked and grave concerns to be raised about how it manages its finances. This complete lack of internal control and consequence management is unacceptable.”

a3949.speaker: Darren Bergman, DA MP
a3949.speech: Said the department had several missions abroad but was being held ransom by the Department of Home Affairs on when and how consular services were delivered: “We must outsource our consular services to private companies like many other countries in the world do. Not only will we economise on our wage bill, but our tight budget will also be able to stretch to more worthy causes.
